claims.text: A machine-learning model can be trained using binary phase-diagram-inspired parameters.
The predictive model explicitly incorporates common defect features, including vacancies and interstitial oxygen.
The proposed model will predict the electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than conventional analytical models.
The conductivity-accuracy improvement will occur in both the approximately 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr is typically present as a high-entropy-alloy solid solution.
Quantum localization and electron scattering by defects are prominent in HfNbTaTiZr at approximately 0–200 K.
Phonon scattering dominates transport in HfNbTaTiZr at approximately 300–1200 K.
Defects and oxygen impurities alter the local lattice environment by creating local strain fields and scattering centers.
Defects and oxygen increase electron and phonon scattering relative to an ideal HfNbTaTiZr crystal.
Phase-diagram-inspired parameters can encode microstructural features such as vacancies, interstitial oxygen, and disorder.
Standard analytical conductivity models assume perfect lattices and neglect defect-associated scattering mechanisms.
Accounting for additional scattering mechanisms improves estimates of effective carrier mobility and conductivity.
The defect-aware model will predict lower conductivity than perfect-crystal analytical models.
The predicted conductivity gap relative to perfect-crystal models will be most pronounced at low temperature because transport is more sensitive to defect scattering there.
At high temperature, oxygen-modulated phonon scattering will enlarge the conductivity difference from perfect-crystal predictions.
The proposed model will improve predictive accuracy by a substantial margin over traditional analytical predictions.
Conventional baseline models do not explicitly account for oxygen impurities or other defects.
The proposed approach is applicable from approximately 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The approach applies to samples containing defect populations representative of manufacturing conditions, including up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.

A failure to reduce conductivity-prediction error significantly relative to the conventional model, or a failure to observe the predicted oxygen-associated conductivity reduction, would falsify the hypothesis.
